title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people according to the time of day, introduce yourself, and choose between *du* and *Sie* — the first decision you have to make every time you open your mouth in German.
bekal: give your name (*Ich heiße…*) and ask someone else's
say who you are (*Ich bin Student*)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — In der Sprachschule
dialogs.intro: The first day of a language course in Berlin. Budi is waiting in the hallway when someone sits down next to him. Read the German out loud first, then glance at the translation.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm Budi. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Freut mich auch. Bist du Student?
lines.id: Nice to meet you too. Are you a student?

lines.text: Ja, ich bin Student. Und du? Bist du Lehrerin?
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. And you? Are you a teacher?

notes: **All nouns are capitalized.** *Student*, *Lehrerin*, *Morgen* — not just at the start of a sentence, but everywhere. This rule has no exceptions in German, and copying it from the very first line is much cheaper than fixing it later.
**Jobs take no article.** *Ich bin Student*, not *ich bin ein Student*. This is where German differs from English, which demands *a student*.

**Women get their own form.** Almost every job title adds **-in** for a woman: *Student → Studentin*, *Lehrer → Lehrerin*, *Arzt → Ärztin*. Lena says *Studentin* because she's a woman; Budi says *Student*.

**Negating a noun uses *kein*, not *nicht*.** *Ich bin **keine** Lehrerin* — not *ich bin nicht Lehrerin*. The full rule comes in Unit 5; for now just learn the pairs: *kein Student*, *keine Lehrerin*.

***Wie geht es dir?*** literally means "how goes it to-you?" — and the answer isn't about you either, but about "it": *Danke, gut*. In quick conversation people shorten it to *Wie geht's?* To someone you address as *Sie*, it's *Wie geht es Ihnen?*

**Greetings follow the time of day.** *Guten Morgen* until about ten, *Guten Tag* through the day, *Guten Abend* after sunset. *Gute Nacht* is only for parting before bed — never for saying hello. In southern Germany and Austria you'll often hear *Grüß Gott* in place of all of them.

grammars.title: The verb sein (to be) — the most important verb in German
body: *Sein* expresses **identity and state** — who you are, what you do, how you feel. Its forms are irregular and look nothing like each other, so it's better to learn them whole now than piece by piece:
after: The last three forms are written together on purpose so you can see the pattern: *wir*, *sie* (they) and *Sie* (formal you) always use exactly the same form throughout German. This rule is never broken, for any verb.
To make a yes/no question, just **move the verb to the front**: *Du bist Student* → *Bist du Student?* There's no helper verb like English *do*, and no extra question word.

grammars.title: du or Sie? A decision you can't avoid
body: German forces its speakers to choose from the very first word: address the other person as **du** (informal) or **Sie** (polite). Choosing wrong won't make you misunderstood, but it stands out — a bit like calling your future in-laws "dude".

head: du
Sie
rows: adult strangers, bosses, officials, shop staff

after: **Sie** is always capitalized, wherever it stands — that's what sets it apart from *sie* ("she" / "they"), which sounds exactly the same. In conversation, your ear tells them apart by the verb form and the tone of the situation, not by the sound.

The practical rule: **when in doubt, use *Sie***. A German who feels too formally treated will offer *Wir können uns duzen* ("we can say du to each other"), and only then do you switch. Using *du* with someone who expects *Sie* is rarely corrected — but it's noted.

blocks.text: This list is best learned whole rather than word by word. They're all fixed phrases that never change form.

⚠️ Unlike English *How are you?*, *Wie geht's?* is not just empty small talk. Germans tend to answer it honestly — even if the answer is *nicht so gut*. Don't be surprised if your polite question gets a short story in reply.

sections.title: Spelling your name: the German alphabet

blocks.text: You'll almost certainly be asked to spell your name — in class, at an office, on the phone. The question is *Wie schreibt man das?* ("how does one write that?") or *Können Sie das buchstabieren?*
Four extra letters: **Ä** ("A-umlaut"), **Ö** ("O-umlaut"), **Ü** ("U-umlaut"), and **ß**, spelled *eszett* or *scharfes S*. If your keyboard has no ß, writing it as **ss** is accepted everywhere.
The two letters beginners mix up most: **V** is called "fow" but sounds like *f*, while **W** is called "vay" and sounds like *v*. So *Wagen* sounds like "VAH-gen", and *Vater* like "FAH-tuh".
